extracted.intended_audience: general newspaper readers interested in wartime labor, economic, and naval policy
extracted.subtask_description: A newspaper news report summarizing wartime legislative debate (Smith-Connally anti-strike bill), executive veto rationale, labor/industry reactions, Justice Dept. findings on the Elk Hills oil contract, and Navy testimony on oil reserves and technology (radar).

rubrics_metrics.name: Section eight — strike notice to government agencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Requires the representatives of employees of a war contractor to give notice of a labor dispute which threatens seriously to interrupt war production to the Secretary of Labor, the National War Labor Board and the National Labor Relations Board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose is to give employees the opportunity to express themselves by secret ballot and to insure continuity of war production; text notes thirty days before NLRB takes a ballot and that the requirement may open controversies over bargaining units and produce unrest rather than cooling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandatory government-administered strike ballot (thirtieth-day secret ballot)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section eight provides that the National Labor Relations Board on the thirtieth day after the giving of the notice take a secret ballot among the employees in the gaining unit or bargaining unit to determine who are for or against the strike.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bill would force a labor leader who is trying to prevent a strike to give the notice which would cause the taking of a strike ballot; critics warn the thirty-day pre-ballot period might become a 'boiling period' and open disputes over bargaining-unit jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of selective service to deter strikes
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommendation to amend the Selective Service Act so that persons who engage in strikes or stoppages in war plants might be inducted into non-combat military service up to the age of sixty-five.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a deterrent to interruption of war production; the proposal met with cool reception in Congress and labor circles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Penalties for strike-related defiance (dues check-off suspension/treasury freezing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed penalties for violations or defiance might take the form of suspension of the dues check-off or freezing of the United Mine Workers treasury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offered as a mechanism to punish or deter strikes in war industries; discussed as one of possible enforcement tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section nine — prohibition on political contributions by labor organizations during war
rubrics_metrics.description: Section nine of the bill prohibits, for the period of the war, political contributions by labor organizations to prevent the use of production for vote getting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Framed as preventing uses of war-time production for political purposes; commentators argued if meritorious it should not be confined to war time and might extend to other non-profit organizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: War Labor Board (WLB) enforcement expectation
rubrics_metrics.description: The War Labor Board is expected to control and enforce management of mines and war plants and to prevent defiance of WLB decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Full compliance would mean operators obey WLB orders; historically some large operators (e.g., U.S. Steel, General Motors) complied reluctantly; the WLB's enforcement role is cited as an alternative to broad new legislation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on reopening certain wage clauses / interim contract protections
rubrics_metrics.description: Board actions and interim contracts may permit reopening of wage clauses under certain conditions, but the Smith-Connally provisions and WLB actions influence whether wage clauses can be reopened during wartime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discussion includes that some contracts contained no-strike pledges for the duration of the war and that reopening wage clauses could be a flashpoint; the board's determinations affect interim settlements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice Department finding — Elk Hills contract illegal/invalid
rubrics_metrics.description: Justice Department report called the Elk Hills contract with Standard Oil 'a masterpiece of equivocation' and found it 'illegal and invalid' under the Oil Conservation Act of 1938 and the War Powers Acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This legal conclusion underpins Congressional and Navy Committee actions; the report's wording warned against imputations of collusion and recommended corrective measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies for improper government contracts (purchase, condemnation, joint development, accounting/damages)
rubrics_metrics.description: Options cited for dealing with the Elk Hills contract: purchase Standard's property, condemn/acquire Standard's interest, or arrange joint development; Standard should cease activities under the contract and be required to account for crude oil extracted and for damages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Condemnation was noted as likely to involve posting large sums and long litigation; officials urged prompt action rather than protracted legalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: National oil-reserve policy — conserve and expand reserves
rubrics_metrics.description: Navy testimony urged the immediate conservation of crude oil, maintenance of storage of oil in the ground, and expansion of the national reserve (including continental U.S. reserves) to avoid projected shortages later in the year or next year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secretary Knox emphasized 'no time for legalisms' and said national policy dictates expanding reserves and increasing sources of supply; recommended immediate attention to conservation measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immediate action on food price rollback and subsidies
rubrics_metrics.description: Calls for prompt enactment and operation of an effective rollback and subsidy program for food (meats, butter, coffee) by a set deadline (e.g., July 15) to prevent inflation and labor unrest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Labor warned it could demand scrapping hold-the-line orders and wage formulas if subsidies and rollback not effective; proponents argued subsidies would transfer some consumer costs to the public treasury but help stabilize prices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place food program under Price Control / centralized food administration
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposal (Senator O'Mahoney) to place the entire food program under the Price Control Act and under a War Food Administrator (a 'food czar') with authority over production, distribution, rationing and prices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Debate included objections about centralization, concerns about inflation vs. control, and Roosevelt's expressed reservations about vesting complete authority in a single czar; supporters argued it would help stabilize supplies and prices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational security in military incident reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Military releases (e.g., submarine sinking) may be withheld until salvage or recovery attempts are discontinued to avoid giving information to the enemy that could endanger salvage vessels or operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Navy withheld announcement of R-12 sinking for operational security; cited to justify temporary non-disclosure of losses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technology adoption by demonstration and industry partnership (radar example)
rubrics_metrics.description: To gain acceptance for new military technologies (radar), prototype demonstration at sea and close cooperation with private industry are necessary—develop prototypes in labs, then have private companies produce operational sets for fleet installation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accounts show demonstration convinced skeptical ship captains and officers; early installations on battleships and carriers helped win acceptance and justify rapid scaling with industry partners.
